96 Plus, China supercharges its navy, economists question GDP figures and a WSJ reporter reveals his family’s immigration secrets.   Is this email difficult to read? View in browser                 Lingling Wei   China Stock Market’s Hidden Problem: Foreign Investors Get a Different Truth   Plus, China supercharges its navy, economists question GDP figures and a WSJ reporter reveals his family’s immigration secrets.     CFOTO/ZUMA PRESS   China’s stock market has just entered bear-market territory, with the blue-chip index down more than 20% from its June peak. Morgan Stanley is warning of another 10% to 15% decline before things bottom out. State-backed funds have rushed in to buy, but the intervention looks more like a Band-Aid than a cure.

   The pain has spread well beyond the mainland. Foreign investors have taken hits through U.S.-listed Chinese stocks, Hong Kong-traded shares, and the Stock Connect programs that have let global investors since 2014 buy directly into mainland markets through Hong Kong brokers. 

   China wants foreign capital. But a new study suggests that Chinese companies aren’t necessarily willing to give foreign investors the same information they provide to domestic shareholders, putting them at a deliberate information disadvantage.

   Published in The Accounting Review, a leading academic journal focused on financial disclosure, the study uses machine-learning tools to compare the Chinese- and English-language versions of annual reports filed by Chinese companies.

   These are supposed to be the same documents in two different languages, but they’re often not, according to a team of researchers—Tina Lang, Lorien Stice-Lawrence, Forester Wong, and T.J. Wong—who wrote the study.

   The English versions provide less complete information overall, the study finds. For instance, it notes, companies with more foreign investors are less likely to mention operations in Xinjiang in their English reports—precisely because those investors are more likely to care about forced-labor allegations. And companies receiving government subsidies play down related-party transactions in English, according to the study, because Western investors tend to see cozy government ties as a governance red flag, while Chinese investors often view them as an advantage. 

   The authors found examples of Chinese-language reports containing details on Communist Party connections, affiliations with the United Front Work Department, a far-reaching party influence operation, and links to companies embroiled in corruption scandals that simply don’t appear in the English version.

   Meanwhile, when Chinese firms want to raise capital from foreign investors—by listing in the U.S. or issuing shares in Hong Kong—they emphasize reassurances about accounting methods in their English reports, the study says, seeking to soothe the concerns foreign investors are most likely to have.

   The researchers didn’t stop at public filings. They ran a field experiment, emailing Chinese firms while posing as both local and foreign investors asking for information. The firms were half as likely to respond to the “foreign” investor. And this response gap was significantly worse for companies with the biggest translation gaps in their public reports, the researchers found.

   Chinese companies pay a price.   Even being a native Chinese speaker doesn’t help if you’re working for a foreign firm. The study found that professional analysts at foreign brokerages end up with worse information and make less accurate forecasts than their Chinese peers. This is largely because companies are reluctant to talk to them and answer their questions, even though most of those analysts speak fluent Mandarin.

   The researchers found that this kind of selective disclosure makes a company’s stock less liquid, meaning it’s harder and more expensive for the firm to raise capital. They’re paying a real price for keeping foreign investors in the dark.

   So why do it? The study identifies two forces at work. One is strategic: firms tailor information to each audience, emphasizing what that group wants to hear and burying what it doesn’t. The other is cultural: in-group favoritism, reinforced by the importance in China of keeping local stakeholders happy, especially government officials, often at the expense of shareholders.

   Previous research has shown that Chinese firms will sometimes take steps to help a connected firm or benefit the government even though those measures might hurt shareholder value. State-owned enterprises comprise most of China’s market capitalization and command outsize regulatory influence. That’s a very different proposition for American investors.

   This contradiction—wanting foreign capital while reflexively protecting insiders—mirrors a tension at the heart of China’s economic model. It’s the same tension visible in the current stock-market rout, where Beijing is simultaneously trying to stabilize stock prices and tightening its grip on the information environment.

   Stice-Lawrence, one of the lead researchers, calls the translation gaps a “canary in the coal mine.” The differences in public filings themselves aren’t the biggest problem. In 2026, any investor can run a Chinese annual report through a translation tool. The bigger issue is what those gaps signal about the private interactions that are far harder to quantify: the phone calls that don’t get returned, and the meetings where less gets shared.

   The researchers aren’t saying don’t invest in China. But as they put it, American and Chinese investors and firms are “playing different games with different rules.” If your strategy depends on having the same information as local investors, you need a different strategy—or a different market.

   Question to readers: Beijing wants foreign capital but won’t give foreign investors equal access to information. How long can it have both? Write to me at lingling.wei@wsj.com . Include your full name and location, and I might publish your response in a coming issue (if you’re reading this in your inbox, you can just hit reply).

Brown, Utah

Regardless of what is actually discussed internally, the public perception will be that he is at the center of mediating the issue and it will reflect positively on him and China. Buzzword

 

“Dalifornia”

Reader Responses

 

Last week, we asked what you would be watching for if a trilateral summit among President Trump, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping actually happens. Readers shared their thoughts:

Brown, Utah

A Name in the News

 
 
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang speaks to the media at the Great Hall of the People in Beijing. GO NAKAMURA/POOL/ASSOCIATED PRESS
 

Alice Huang, a data-center industry executive with close ties to Nvidia’s CEO Jensen Huang, has been investigated in the U.S., Singapore and Taiwan over allegations that she doubled as a Chinese intelligence source and diverted critical AI chips to Beijing, according to people familiar with the matter.
